strengths: The task is practically motivated: reference images provide identity and stable appearance information, while relative captions describe changes. SynCPR’s 1.15 million synthetic triplets and ITCPR’s 2,202 queries against 20,510 gallery images could become useful community resources.

The experiments provide convincing evidence that domain-specific synthetic training data helps. Training on SynCPR improves SPRC’s Rank-1 accuracy from 25.07% to 42.27% and CaLa’s from 24.02% to 39.33% on ITCPR.

FAFA improves over methods trained on the same data: it achieves 46.54% Rank-1 and 55.60% mAP, compared with SPRC’s 42.27% and 51.62%. The supplementary CIRR results provide additional evidence beyond the proposed benchmark, with Rank-1 improving from SPRC’s 51.96% to 54.48%.

The presentation is generally clear, with explicit objectives, useful pipeline illustrations, detailed generation/filtering prompts, training settings, and component ablations. Generating paired images within one canvas is a sensible practical approach to encouraging identity consistency.
weaknesses: The main concern is evaluation independence. Section 4.3 and Appendix C.4 describe selecting the soft-label strength, top-k value, filtering threshold, loss weights, and masking ratio according to ITCPR performance, while Appendix B.1.3 designates ITCPR exclusively for testing. No separate validation set or independent selection procedure is reported. This apparent test-set tuning undermines confidence in the central results and is the strongest reason against acceptance.

The central synthetic-data quality claims lack independent verification. A single MLLM’s averaged scores and selected visual examples do not establish identity consistency or caption correctness; averaging also allows weaknesses in one criterion to be compensated by others. There is no quantitative human audit or controlled downstream comparison isolating joint image generation and LoRA adaptation. Claims of comprehensive ethnic representation and superior coverage are likewise unsupported by measurements.

ITCPR’s annotation reliability is insufficiently established. Appendix B.1.2 uses SOLIDER’s top-k neighbors to identify additional positives, but does not specify k, audit coverage, or annotator agreement. This procedure does not substantiate the claim that false negatives have been eliminated. Results broken down by the three source datasets would also help establish whether improvements are consistent across distinct acquisition conditions.

Methodological novelty and attribution need stronger support. FAFA combines established BLIP-2 representations, top-k matching, diversity regularization, and masked reconstruction. The FDA-versus-ITC ablation changes multiple ingredients together, while image-only/text-only controls trained on SynCPR are missing. Prior synthetic-triplet and quality-assessment approaches deserve closer comparison. No repeated-run variability or confidence intervals are reported, particularly limiting interpretation of the small auxiliary-loss gains.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful appendix details. The MFR decoder architecture, feature/query dimensions, and batch construction governing exposure to shared-GID examples are not sufficiently specified. These affect central training objectives. The promised code and data release does not resolve these omissions within the manuscript.

The privacy motivation needs a concrete ethical discussion. The generator is fine-tuned on real person images, and ITCPR contains identifiable people, yet source-data permissions, redistribution conditions, and risks of nonconsensual identity tracking are not addressed. Synthetic generation alone does not settle these questions; this is a documentation gap rather than evidence of misconduct.
